subject: math
title: Grade 2 Money: Coins to 100¢, Spending and Saving
seo_title: Grade 2 Money Worksheets: Canadian Coins to 100¢, Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Financial literacy – coin combinations to 100 cents, and spending and saving
meta_desc: Free Grade 2 math worksheets on Canadian coins for the BC curriculum: learn coin values, count nickels, dimes, quarters and loonies to 100¢, make the same amount in different ways, use the fewest coins and save for a $1 goal. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Count coins by value, not by the number of coins.
key_sub: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢. To reach a $1 goal, count up to 100¢.
body_html:
Canadian coins

Learn the name and the value of each coin. Size does not tell you the value. The dime is the smallest coin, but it is worth more than the nickel.

CoinValueGood to know
nickel5¢2 nickels = 1 dime
dime10¢10 dimes = 100¢
quarter25¢4 quarters = 100¢
loonie$1 = 100¢11 sides, gold colour

Count the coins, biggest first

Put the coins in order, biggest value first. Then count on.

Example

Count 3 quarters and 2 dimes.

25¢, 50¢, 75¢, then 85¢, 95¢.

Answer: 95¢

The same amount in different ways

50¢ can be 2 quarters, or 5 dimes, or 1 quarter, 2 dimes and 1 nickel. 100¢ can be 1 loonie, 4 quarters or 10 dimes.

For the fewest coins, use the biggest coin you can each time. 30¢ is 1 quarter and 1 nickel: only 2 coins.

Example

Show 75¢ in two ways.

3 quarters: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢. Or 7 dimes and 1 nickel: 70¢, 75¢.

Answer: 3 quarters, or 7 dimes and 1 nickel

Spending and saving

Spending means using money to buy something now. Saving means keeping money to use later. A saving goal tells you how much you need. To find how much more you need, count up to the goal.

Example

Kai has 60¢ for a $1 goal. He spends 20¢ on a sticker. How much more does he need now?

60¢ − 20¢ = 40¢. From 40¢ to 100¢ is 60¢.

Answer: 60¢

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
4 coins, so 4¢Count the value of each coin: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢
A quarter is 20¢A quarter is 25¢. Four quarters make 100¢
The nickel is bigger, so it is worth moreThe small dime is 10¢. The nickel is 5¢
Start with the small coinsStart with the biggest coin, then count on
Add to find how much more you needCount up from what you have to the goal

faq.q: What do Grade 2 students learn about money in BC?
faq.a: The BC Grade 2 math curriculum lists “coin combinations to 100 cents, and spending and saving” under Financial literacy. Students count nickels, dimes, quarters and loonies to 100¢, make the same amount in different ways and talk about spending and saving.

faq.q: How do I help my child count coins?
faq.a: Sort the coins and start with the biggest value, then count on: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 65¢. Use real coins at home and say the value of each one, not just the number of coins.

faq.q: Why are there no pennies in Canada?
faq.a: Canada stopped giving out pennies in 2013. Cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5¢, so the nickel is the smallest coin children count.

faq.q: How can I teach my child about saving money?
faq.a: Choose a small goal, like $1 for a toy, and use a jar or piggy bank. Each week, count the coins together and ask how much more is needed to reach the goal.

items.q: What is this coin called?
items.e: This is a nickel. It is worth 5¢. It is bigger than a dime, but worth less.

items.q: What is this coin called?
items.e: This is a dime. It is worth 10¢. It is the smallest coin.

items.q: What is this coin called?
items.e: This is a quarter. It is worth 25¢.

items.q: What is this coin called?
items.e: This is a loonie. It is gold in colour and has 11 sides. It is worth $1, or 100¢.

items.q: What is this coin called?
items.e: This is a toonie. It has a silver ring and a gold centre. It is worth $2.

items.q: How much is a nickel worth?
items.e: A nickel is worth 5¢. Two nickels make a dime.

items.q: How much is a dime worth?
items.e: A dime is worth 10¢. It is small, but it is worth more than a nickel.

items.q: How much is a quarter worth?
items.e: A quarter is worth 25¢, not 20¢. Four quarters make 100¢.

items.q: A loonie is worth $1. How many cents is that?
items.e: $1 is 100¢. So a loonie is worth 100¢.

items.q: Which coin is worth 25¢?
items.e: A quarter is worth 25¢.

items.q: Which coin is worth 100¢?
items.e: 100¢ is $1. A loonie is worth $1. A toonie is worth $2, or 200¢.

items.q: Which coin is worth more?
items.e: The dime is worth 10¢. The nickel is worth 5¢. A bigger coin is not always worth more.

items.q: Which coin is worth the least?
items.e: Nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, loonie 100¢. The nickel is worth the least.

items.q: Which coin is worth the most?
items.e: Nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢. The quarter is worth the most.

items.q: How many nickels make a dime?
items.e: A nickel is 5¢. 5¢ + 5¢ = 10¢. So 2 nickels make a dime.

items.q: How many nickels make a quarter?
items.e: Count by 5s: 5¢, 10¢, 15¢, 20¢, 25¢. That is 5 nickels. 4 nickels make only 20¢.

items.q: How many dimes make 50¢?
items.e: Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢. That is 5 dimes.

items.q: How many quarters make 100¢?
items.e: Count by 25s: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. That is 4 quarters. 5 is right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: How many dimes make 100¢?
items.e: Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢ … 100¢. That is 10 dimes.

items.q: Which is worth more: 1 quarter or 2 dimes?
items.e: 1 quarter is 25¢. 2 dimes are 10¢ + 10¢ = 20¢. 25¢ is more, so 1 quarter is worth more. 2 coins are not always worth more than 1 coin.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each dime is 10¢. Count by 10¢: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢. That is 30¢. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins. 3¢ counts the coins, not the cents.

items.q: Hana has these coins. How much does she have?
items.e: Each nickel is 5¢. Count by 5¢: 5¢, 10¢, 15¢, 20¢. That is 20¢. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins. 4¢ counts the coins, not the cents.

items.q: Simran finds these coins in her backpack. How much is it?
items.e: Each quarter is 25¢. Count by 25¢: 25¢, 50¢. That is 50¢. Count the value of each coin, not the number of coins. 2¢ counts the coins, not the cents. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢.

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Each dime is 10¢. Count by 10¢: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢, 60¢. That is 60¢. 6¢ counts the coins, not the cents.

items.q: Arjun puts these coins in a piggy bank. How much is in the bank?
items.e: Each nickel is 5¢. Count by 5¢: 5¢, 10¢, 15¢, 20¢, 25¢, 30¢, 35¢. That is 35¢. 7¢ counts the coins, not the cents.

items.q: Jasleen finds these coins in her backpack. How much is it?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 70¢, 80¢. That is 80¢. 5¢ counts the coins, not the cents. A quarter is 25¢, not 20¢.

sets.title: Make the same amount in different ways

items.q: Which is worth the same as these coins?
items.e: Each nickel is 5¢. Count by 5¢: 5¢, 10¢. That is 10¢. 1 dime also makes 10¢.

items.q: Which coins make 20¢?
items.e: 1 dime and 2 nickels make 20¢. 1 dime and 1 nickel make 15¢. 5 nickels make 25¢. 3 dimes make 30¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as these coins?
items.e: Each dime is 10¢. Count by 10¢: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢. That is 50¢. 2 quarters also make 50¢.

items.q: Which coins make 35¢?
items.e: 1 quarter and 1 dime make 35¢. 1 quarter and 1 nickel make 30¢. 4 dimes make 40¢. 2 quarters make 50¢.

items.q: Which coins make 50¢?
items.e: 2 quarters make 50¢. 1 quarter and 2 dimes make 45¢. 3 dimes make 30¢. 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢.

items.q: Which does not make 25¢?
items.e: 3 dimes make 30¢, not 25¢. The others all make 25¢.

items.q: Noah has 3 coins. They make 45¢. Which coins does he have?
items.e: 1 quarter and 2 dimes make 45¢. 1 quarter, 1 dime and 1 nickel make 40¢. 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢. 3 dimes make 30¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as these coins?
items.e: Start with the biggest coin and count on: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢. That is 60¢. 6 dimes also make 60¢.

items.q: Which does not make 60¢?
items.e: 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢, not 60¢. The others all make 60¢.

items.q: Which coins make 65¢?
items.e: 2 quarters, 1 dime and 1 nickel make 65¢. 2 quarters and 1 dime make 60¢. 1 quarter, 2 dimes and 1 nickel make 50¢. 3 quarters and 1 nickel make 80¢.

items.q: Which coins make 75¢?
items.e: 3 quarters make 75¢. 2 quarters and 2 dimes make 70¢. 2 quarters and 1 dime make 60¢. 4 quarters make 100¢.

items.q: 2 quarters and some dimes make 70¢. How many dimes?
items.e: 2 quarters: 25¢, 50¢. From 50¢ to 70¢ is 20¢. 20¢ is 2 dimes. 3 dimes comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: Which does not make 80¢?
items.e: 3 quarters make 75¢, not 80¢. The others all make 80¢.

items.q: Ava has 4 coins. They make 55¢. Which coins does she have?
items.e: 1 quarter and 3 dimes make 55¢. 1 quarter, 2 dimes and 1 nickel make 50¢. 4 dimes make 40¢. 2 quarters and 1 dime make 60¢.

items.q: Which coins make 90¢?
items.e: 3 quarters, 1 dime and 1 nickel make 90¢. 3 quarters and 1 dime make 85¢. 3 quarters and 1 nickel make 80¢. 4 quarters make 100¢.

items.q: Sofia has 1 quarter and 5 dimes. Nadia has 3 quarters. Who has more money?
items.e: Sofia: 25¢, then 35¢, 45¢, 55¢, 65¢, 75¢. Nadia: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢. Both have 75¢, so they have the same. Sofia has more coins, but not more money.

items.q: 3 quarters and some nickels make 100¢. How many nickels?
items.e: 3 quarters: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢. From 75¢ to 100¢ is 25¢. Count by 5s: 80¢, 85¢, 90¢, 95¢, 100¢. That is 5 nickels. 8 comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: Which is worth the same as these coins?
items.e: One loonie is 100¢. 10 dimes also make 100¢.

items.q: Which does not make 100¢?
items.e: 3 quarters and 2 dimes make 95¢, not 100¢. The others all make 100¢.

items.q: Which coins make 100¢, the same as a loonie?
items.e: 2 quarters and 5 dimes make 100¢. 2 quarters and 4 dimes make 90¢. 3 quarters and 1 dime make 85¢. 1 quarter and 5 dimes make 75¢.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 15¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 1 dime and 1 nickel make 15¢. That is 2 coins. Three nickels work, but that is 3 coins. 15 coins counts cents, not coins.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 20¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 2 dimes make 20¢. That is 2 coins. Four nickels work, but 2 dimes is fewer.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 25¢?
items.e: All of these make 25¢. 1 quarter uses only 1 coin. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 30¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 1 quarter and 1 nickel make 30¢. That is 2 coins. There is no 30¢ coin. Three dimes work, but 2 coins is fewer.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 35¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 1 quarter and 1 dime make 35¢. That is 2 coins. Three dimes and a nickel work, but that is 4 coins.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 40¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 1 quarter, 1 dime and 1 nickel make 40¢. That is 3 coins. Four dimes work, but a quarter, a dime and a nickel is only 3 coins.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 45¢?
items.e: All of these make 45¢. 1 quarter and 2 dimes use only 3 coins. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 50¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 2 quarters make 50¢. That is 2 coins. Five dimes work, but 2 quarters is fewer.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 55¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 2 quarters and 1 nickel make 55¢. That is 3 coins. Two coins make only 50¢. You need 1 more coin, a nickel.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 60¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 2 quarters and 1 dime make 60¢. That is 3 coins. Six dimes work, but that is 6 coins.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 65¢?
items.e: All of these make 65¢. 2 quarters, 1 dime and 1 nickel use only 4 coins. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 70¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 2 quarters and 2 dimes make 70¢. That is 4 coins. Seven dimes work, but that is 7 coins. Three coins can make 60¢ or 75¢, but not 70¢.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 75¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 3 quarters make 75¢. That is 3 coins. Seven dimes and a nickel work, but that is 8 coins. 4 is right only if a quarter were 20¢.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 80¢?
items.e: All of these make 80¢. 3 quarters and 1 nickel use only 4 coins. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 85¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 3 quarters and 1 dime make 85¢. That is 4 coins. Three quarters make 75¢. Add 1 dime: 85¢. Without quarters you need many more coins.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 90¢?
items.e: All of these make 90¢. 3 quarters, 1 dime and 1 nickel use only 5 coins. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 95¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 3 quarters and 2 dimes make 95¢. That is 5 coins. Three quarters make 75¢. Add 2 dimes: 85¢, 95¢.

items.q: You have no loonie. What is the smallest number of coins you can use to make 100¢?
items.e: Use the biggest coin you can each time: 4 quarters make 100¢. That is 4 coins. Ten dimes work, but that is 10 coins. A loonie is 1 coin, but this time you have no loonie.

items.q: Which uses the fewest coins to make 100¢?
items.e: All of these make 100¢. 1 loonie uses only 1 coin. Start with the biggest coin you can.

items.q: You want to make 70¢ with the fewest coins. Which coin do you use first?
items.e: Use the biggest coin that is not more than 70¢. A loonie is 100¢, too much. So start with a quarter: 25¢, 50¢, then 2 dimes: 60¢, 70¢.

items.q: What does saving money mean?
items.e: Saving means keeping money to use later, so you can buy something you want.

items.q: Hana’s saving goal is $1. How many cents is that?
items.e: $1 = 100¢. That is the same as 4 quarters or 10 dimes.

items.q: Simran is saving for a $1 goal. She has 60¢. How much more does she need?
items.e: Count up from 60¢: 70¢, 80¢, 90¢, 100¢. That is 4 tens. She needs 40¢ more. 160¢ adds instead of finding the difference.

items.q: Ryan is saving for a $1 goal. He has these coins. How much more does he need?
items.e: Count: 25¢, 50¢, 60¢, 70¢. Ryan has 70¢. 70¢ + 30¢ = 100¢, so he needs 30¢ more. 40¢ comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: Arjun saves 1 quarter each week. How many weeks until he has $1?
items.e: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢. After 4 weeks he has $1. 5 weeks comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: Mei saves 1 dime each day. How many days until she has $1?
items.e: Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢ … 100¢. That is 10 days. 5 days would give only 50¢.

items.q: Chloe has 80¢. She spends 35¢ on a freezie. How much does she have left?
items.e: 80¢ − 35¢: 80¢ − 30¢ = 50¢. 50¢ − 5¢ = 45¢. Check: 35¢ + 45¢ = 80¢. 55¢ comes from taking 0 − 5 as 5. 115¢ adds instead of taking away.

items.q: Ethan has 100¢. He is saving it for a $1 comic book. If he spends 50¢ on gum today, can he still buy the comic book?
items.e: 100¢ − 50¢ = 50¢. The comic book costs 100¢, so no, he will have only 50¢. Spending now means less for the goal.

items.q: Lucas buys a granola bar and a freezie. How much does he spend?
items.e: 45¢ + 25¢: 40¢ + 20¢ = 60¢. 5¢ + 5¢ = 10¢. 60¢ + 10¢ = 70¢. 60¢ forgets the extra 10¢. 20¢ is the difference, not the total.

items.q: Wei has 75¢. Which two snacks cost exactly 75¢?
items.e: Juice box and freezie: 50¢ + 25¢ = 75¢. Apple and granola bar make 80¢. Apple and freezie make 60¢. Granola bar and juice box make 95¢.

items.q: Emma has these coins. A juice box costs 50¢. Can she buy it?
items.e: Count: 25¢, 35¢, 45¢, 55¢, 60¢. Emma has 60¢. 60¢ − 50¢ = 10¢, so yes, with 10¢ left. 5¢ left comes from counting the quarter as 20¢.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Leah gives 3 quarters. How much does she give?
items.e: Count by 25s: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢. Leah gives 75¢. 60¢ counts a quarter as 20¢. 3¢ counts the coins.

items.q: At Jasleen’s lemonade stand, a cup costs 20¢. She sells 4 cups. How much money does she get?
items.e: Count by 20s: 20¢, 40¢, 60¢, 80¢. 4 cups make 80¢. 24¢ adds 20 + 4. 60¢ is only 3 cups.

items.q: Harjot has saved 45¢. His grandpa gives him 2 quarters. Does he reach his $1 goal?
items.e: 2 quarters are 50¢. 45¢ + 50¢ = 95¢. 95¢ + 5¢ = 100¢, so no, he needs 5¢ more. 15¢ more comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.

items.q: Liam wants a $1 bouncy ball. He has 40¢. He saves 20¢ each week. How many weeks until he has $1?
items.e: Count on by 20s from 40¢: 60¢, 80¢, 100¢. That is 3 weeks. 5 weeks forgets the 40¢ he already has.

items.q: Zara has a loonie. She spends 65¢ at the school bake sale. How much is left?
items.e: A loonie is 100¢. Count up from 65¢: 70¢ is 5¢, then 100¢ is 30¢ more. 5¢ + 30¢ = 35¢. 45¢ is a regrouping mistake. 165¢ adds instead of taking away.

items.q: Kai saves 1 dime every day for 7 days. How much has he saved?
items.e: Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢, 60¢, 70¢. He has 70¢. 35¢ counts the dimes as nickels. 7¢ counts the coins.

items.q: Mateo has 85¢ for a $1 goal. He spends 25¢ on a treat. How much more does he need now?
items.e: 85¢ − 25¢ = 60¢. From 60¢ to 100¢ is 40¢. Before the treat, he needed only 15¢. Spending moves you away from your goal.

items.q: On a class trip to the Vancouver Aquarium, Owen has 90¢ for the gift shop. He buys a pencil for 55¢. How much is left?
items.e: 90¢ − 55¢: 90¢ − 50¢ = 40¢. 40¢ − 5¢ = 35¢. Check: 55¢ + 35¢ = 90¢. 45¢ comes from taking 0 − 5 as 5. 145¢ adds instead of taking away.

items.q: Olivia is saving for a $1 kite. She has these coins. How much more does she need?
items.e: Count: 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 85¢, 90¢, 95¢. Olivia has 95¢. 95¢ + 5¢ = 100¢, so she needs 5¢ more. 20¢ comes from counting a quarter as 20¢.
